headline: New Law Opens Path to Clean Up Thousands of Toxic Mines
meta_description: EPA issues first permit under 2024 Good Samaritan Act, letting nonprofits clean up abandoned mines without legal liability. Trout Unlimited tackles Washington'…
summary_short: For the first time, a nonprofit can legally clean up an abandoned mine without becoming liable for remaining pollution. Trout Unlimited received the landmark permit.
body:
For twenty years, environmental groups pushed for a simple change: let someone clean up the mess. On January 1st, that effort paid off. The EPA issued the first permit under the 2024 Good Samaritan Act to Trout Unlimited, a fishing nonprofit, to remediate the Bodie Mine in Okanogan County, Washington—about 140 miles northwest of Spokane. The breakthrough matters because tens of thousands of abandoned mines across the country leak arsenic, lead, cadmium, and mercury into drinking water and streams, yet no one is legally required to fix them. Before this law, organizations that volunteered to clean up these sites faced a cruel paradox: federal law treated them as polluters, not helpers, exposing them to unlimited liability even after they finished the work. The Good Samaritan Act solved that by creating a pilot program offering limited liability protection for up to fifteen low-risk projects.

At Toroda Creek, where the Bodie Mine sits, historic tailings—the grinding residue left behind from ore extraction—will be removed and streambanks restored. The work addresses a century-old wound: toxic heavy metals that were once safely buried underground, ground up during mining, and left in piles on the surface. The project will improve the broader Columbia River Basin watershed, benefiting both fish and human communities downstream.

The law passed with unusual bipartisan backing, championed by senators from New Mexico and Idaho alongside representatives from Utah, Alaska, and Nevada. That coalition reflected a shared recognition: thousands of sites need attention, owners are long dead or impossible to locate, and waiting for legal responsibility to materialize only guarantees more contamination. Now, for the first time, good intentions and real resources can meet without legal fear standing in the way.
quick_facts: EPA issues first Good Samaritan permit to Trout Unlimited for mine cleanup
Bodie Mine in Washington's Okanogan County releases arsenic, lead, cadmium, mercury
2024 law took 20 years of advocacy to pass with bipartisan support
Pilot program protects up to 15 organizations from liability after cleanup
